title: Reasoning effort and context and output limits

opening.headline: When processing a long document, calculate how much the context window, output limit, and inference strength constrain your requirements.
body: The request to read and summarize a 200-page document in one go may seem simple, but there are many considerations to examine during the design phase. It is necessary to verify whether the document fits within the model's working memory, whether the summary exceeds the output limit, and how much input cost accumulates per call.

In this lesson, we examine what context window and output length limits are based on, and how reasoning strength affects limits and costs. We then directly calculate usage based on assumed values, and together with explanations, review design alternatives available when limits are exceeded.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: We can explain the roles of reasoning strength and context window, as well as output limits.
Distinguishes whether requirements can be handled together with their corresponding limits and selects an appropriate design alternative.

screens.title: The limit encountered at the beginning of page 200 of the document
screens.lead: Read the following requirements and think about what needs to be verified before implementing these requirements.

visual.alt: An illustration showing a context box containing a document bundle and a summary output.

paragraphs: The request is this: summarize a 200-page contract document in one go. While this may take a long time for a human, it requires three verifications first for a model.

First, we cannot determine whether the document fits within the model's context window. Second, even if it fits, the summary might exceed the output limit. Third, once the document is included, input token costs are incurred with each call.

Here, the limit is not a function of the model but a constraint of the design. Before asking whether a requirement has a function, we must first determine whether it falls within the defined limits. This course covers the methods for such calculations and alternative solutions when a requirement does not fit within those limits.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is it the same to say that a document has entered the window and that its design is realistic? The class calculation example confirms the answer.

screens.outro: First, let us reflect on your experience with limits encountered.

screens.title: Recall a context boundary violation
screens.lead: When you select a symptom, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Since you haven't entered or submitted an answer, first reflect on whether you've had a similar experience.

items.prompt: Have you ever received a response that seemed like they forgot a previous instruction towards the end of a long conversation?
items.answer: The model does not forget like a human, but rather, as conversations accumulate, tokens fill the context window, leading to decreased accuracy and fidelity, or partial degradation. This phenomenon—where quality deteriorates as the context window grows larger despite increasing token count—is known as context rot. Choosing what to include is therefore critically important.

items.prompt: Have you ever encountered an error stating that the request is too long?
items.answer: This indicates that the input has exceeded the limit. System prompts, all messages, tool definitions, images, and documents collectively may fill the entire window, resulting in actual usage that exceeds the visible content. By counting the token count before sending, you can anticipate this in advance.

items.prompt: Has the response ever been truncated mid-way?
items.answer: This indicates that the output limit has been reached. The output limit is the maximum length that can be generated in a single response and is a separate value from the input limit. Tokens used in reasoning also count toward the output limit, so as the reasoning process becomes longer, the available space for the final response decreases.

screens.outro: Let's compare the context window and output length based on experience.

screens.title: What divides the context window from output limits?
screens.lead: Alternate between the two state buttons to compare how Claude and Gemini display the window and output limits differently.

visual.alt: An illustration showing input, thought, and output simultaneously filling the window, presented in two different notational styles side by side.
labels: System prompt · message · tool definition · documentation

states.label: Claude: Separate window and output display
states.body: In Claude, the context window consists of all text that the model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself. The context window is filled with system prompts, all messages, tool definitions, images and documents, and even extended reasoning. Current models at the five-tier level—Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1—all feature a 1M-token context window and a maximum output of 128K tokens per request. The amount consumed by this request can be viewed in the usage field returned in the response. Even with a large context window, context rot—where accuracy and coherence degrade as token count increases—can still occur, so selecting what to include remains essential.

states.label: Gemini 4 Argon: Unified Limit
states.body: The Gemini 4 Argon documentation specifies the context window as an integrated limit that encompasses both input and output, with a value of 1,048,576 tokens. The maximum output is 65,536 tokens under the default prompting call, and can be extended up to 1,048,575 tokens when using the long output feature. When input size increases, the available space for output within the same window decreases. Therefore, when reading the documentation, you must determine whether the input and output limits are specified separately or combined as a single integrated limit.

screens.outro: This is something that comes to mind. In the next screen, we'll look at the impact of inference strength on limits and costs.

screens.title: Inference strength: Thinking has limits and incurs costs.
screens.lead: Move the slider to adjust the inference strength level. A description shows how quality, latency, and resource usage vary at each level.

visual.alt: A conceptual chart showing that as inference strength increases, quality improves, but so do latency and thought token usage.
labels: This is a conceptual diagram without numbers.

stops.body: It either doesn't think much or thinks briefly and provides answers. It has the shortest delay and lowest cost, and consumes fewer thinking tokens compared to the window and output limits. It is well-suited for tasks where answers are relatively clear, such as classification, extraction, and format transformation. However, it may produce insufficient quality in complex reasoning tasks.

This is the starting point for typical work. In the Claude document, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 55 have a baseline effort level of medium, and we recommend adjusting this up or down based on the evaluation results. Gemini offers thinking levels of low, medium, and high, while OpenAI pairs model types with reasoning effort to determine the appropriate level.

In difficult prompts, quality improves but latency and costs increase, and thought tokens consume more of the model's context window and output limit. In Claude documents, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1 have a high baseline effort. Thoughts are counted as part of max_tokens and billed as output tokens, and are also subject to speed limits.

screens.outro: Now let's calculate the limit as a concrete number.

screens.title: Capacity calculation example: Does the document fit within the window?
screens.lead: The following is an approximation of the usage on page 200 of the document. The number of tokens per page is based on assumptions for explanatory purposes. Read the code and verify, along with the right-hand explanation, what each line is counting.

data.code:
#Assumption: One side is approximately 600 tokens (actual value should be verified by token counting)
PAGES = 200
TOKENS_PER_PAGE = 600
WINDOW = 1_000_000          #Context Window
MAX_OUTPUT = 128_000        #Maximum output

doc = PAGES * TOKENS_PER_PAGE        # 120,000
instruction = 2_000                  #Command statement
summary = 4_000                      #Summary output

input_tokens = doc + instruction     # 122,000
used = input_tokens + summary        # 126,000
print(used <= WINDOW, summary <= MAX_OUTPUT)   # True True

IN_PRICE = 2.0 / 1_000_000           #Sonnet 5.5 Input $2/MTok
cost_one = input_tokens * IN_PRICE   #Price: $0.244
cost_20 = cost_one * 20              #Price: $4.88
print(round(cost_one, 3), round(cost_20, 2))

notes.note: Set the output limit and tokens per page as constants. Assuming 600 tokens per page is a hypothetical value; if incorrectly applied, all subsequent calculations will be off. In actual service scenarios, token counts must be estimated via a token-counting API before sending requests.

Document: 120,000 tokens, Instruction: 2,000 tokens, Summary: 4,000 tokens. If system prompts or tool definitions are present, they must be added to the input; otherwise, the token usage will be underestimated.

A total of 126,000 tokens fits comfortably within a 1M context window, and the summary of 4,000 tokens also fits within the maximum output of 128K. Since both conditions are true, this request is not impossible due to limits.

With an input of 122,000 tokens multiplied by the input cost, each call amounts to approximately $0.244. If the same document is queried 20 times, the input is repeated 20 times, resulting in approximately $4.88. The constraint here is not a limit, but the cost associated with repeated input.

screens.outro: Based on the calculation results, we will illustrate an alternative solution for cases exceeding the limit.

screens.title: Design alternative explanation for exceeding limits
screens.lead: The instructor will now explain the situation where the document has become larger. Select the arrow to proceed step by step, following the order of alternatives and the selection criteria.

steps.title: Situation: The document expands to twice its size and exceeds the window boundaries.
steps.body: In the previous calculation, page 200 amounted to approximately 120,000 tokens. Now, assuming the document has grown significantly such that it exceeds a single window's capacity and summaries have become long enough to be difficult to fit into one go, there are four main design options. The first step is to confirm whether the token limit has indeed been exceeded by counting the token count.

steps.title: Option 1: Split Summary
steps.body: Divide the document into sections or chunks, summarize each section, then recombine the summaries to form a final summary. Since only one input call is made, the limit issue is resolved. However, there is a risk of missing relationships between sections, and the number of calls increases. For summaries that require understanding the overall flow, section boundaries must be carefully chosen.

steps.title: Option 2. Insert only the necessary parts via search
steps.body: If the requirement is to answer questions rather than provide a summary, only relevant portions are retrieved and inserted, reducing input length. Shorter input reduces not only window size but also costs and context rot. However, if retrieval misses relevant content, the answer may become incorrect, making search quality a new constraint.

steps.title: Option 3. Split Output
steps.body: If the output reaches the maximum output limit, it is requested in separate, per-segment requests rather than a single long response. Additionally, since tokens used for thinking also consume the output limit, requests with higher inference intensity should also consider that the remaining space in the response will be smaller.

steps.title: Alternative 4: Reduce repetitive input costs by cost engineering
steps.body: Even if a document is loaded into the window, repeated queries for the same document accumulate input costs. In such cases, cost design strategies like caching or batching reduce the per-unit cost of repeated inputs. These alternatives are not mutually exclusive and can be used together.

steps.title: Selection criterion: Is it used once, or is it repeatedly queried?
steps.body: If the document is summarized only once, a fragmented summary is simple and appropriate. If the same document is queried multiple times, it is better to reduce input via search or caching. In either case, the approach should be to first calculate whether the requirement falls within limits, and then choose an alternative.

screens.outro: I will summarize the relationship between limits and design on the final screen.

screens.title: The limit is a constraint of the design.
screens.lead: This lesson's core is summarized in a single diagram. Please revisit the answer to the question posed in the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: The context window is the working memory that the model references when generating a single response. It includes not only the system prompt, messages, tool definitions, and documents provided as input, but also the model's own generated responses and thoughts, filling the entire window. The output limit refers to the maximum length of a single response, and depending on the model, this limit may either be separate from the context window or shared within a divided context window.

Inference strength is a quality setting that simultaneously affects cost and resource limits. Increasing strength improves performance on difficult problems but increases latency and cost, and reduces the available headroom for thought tokens. Before increasing strength in scenarios with tight resource limits, it is essential to first verify that sufficient headroom remains.

Going back to the initial question, the fact that a document fits within a window is different from the design being practical. Document on page 200 fits adequately within the window, but if the same document is queried 20 times, the input cost accumulates to approximately $4.88. When costs exceed a threshold, responses are handled through partitioning, searching, splitting for output, and cost modeling. Alternatives are determined based on whether the document is used once or is subject to repeated queries.

It's best to perform limit calculations as soon as requirements are received. By listing the longest input, longest output, and call frequency, and then comparing them against the window and output limits, input cost per unit, you immediately identify which requirements pose a risk.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The number of tokens per page and the number of questions in the text are assumptions for illustrative purposes. For actual calculations, replace them with the usage values confirmed through the token counting API.

checks.intro: Check what you've just learned by matching terms with their descriptions. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Pair up the terms and explanations.
right: The phenomenon where accuracy and recall decrease as the number of tokens increases
Configuration that trades intelligence against latency and cost within the same model
The model's working memory that fills in system prompts, messages, tool definitions, and responses
Maximum length achievable in a single response
checks.explain: The window is working memory that holds inputs and outputs, and its output limit is the upper bound of response length. Effort serves as a handle for intelligence, delay, and cost within the same model; even if the window is large, what is ultimately inserted matters due to context rot.

checks.intro: Now that you've reviewed the example explained a moment ago, check for yourself. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: I confirmed that a 200-page document has been loaded into the window. However, repeatedly asking the same question twenty times proved to be a problem. What would be the most appropriate response?
options: Insert the document each time, but reduce the cost of repeated inputs by designing for caching or batching.
The opening is sufficient, so cost considerations are not necessary in the design.
Switching to a larger model removes input costs
Increase the output limit to reduce the number of input tokens per question
checks.explain: Even with entry into the cache, repeated input on each call incurs cost constraints. For repeated queries, cost optimizations such as caching or searches limited to relevant portions can reduce input overhead.

wrong.1: Even within the limit, repeated inputs accumulate as costs.
wrong.2: The window size and input cost are separate; there is a cost associated with input tokens.
wrong.3: The output limit is a cap on response length and is unrelated to the number of input tokens.

glossary.def: This is the total token range referenced when the model generates a single response. It includes both the input and the output generated by the model.
The maximum number of tokens that can be generated from a single response.
A setting that adjusts the amount of thinking performed by the model before generating a response. Balances intelligence with delay and cost.
The phenomenon where accuracy and reproducibility degrade as the number of tokens inside the window increases.

misconceptions.myth: If the window is 1M, then you can just put in any document.
misconceptions.fact: The more you add, the higher the cost may become, and accuracy and reproducibility may decrease. Even with a larger window, you still need to decide what to include.

misconceptions.myth: The input limit and output limit are the same number.
misconceptions.fact: Output has a separate upper limit. The current Claude model has a window of 1M and an output of 128K. Gemini 4 Argon divides the input and output into separate limits.

misconceptions.myth: Inference strength is merely a quality setting.
misconceptions.fact: Thinking tokens are also charged as output tokens, using the window and output limits. Increasing the strength results in higher costs and delays, along with improved quality.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The limit is not a functional constraint but a design constraint and must be determined first through calculation.
The device contains input, processing, and output functions, and the output limit is calculated separately.
Inference strength moves alongside quality, cost, and usage limits.
When the limit is exceeded, respond with installment, search splitting, output splitting, and cost design.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What percentages of the limit are the longest input and longest output among my requirements?
